description: I’m a second-year technology student passionate about AI, software development, entrepreneurship, and space technology. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, I’m developing AgroShift AI, a platform using NASA Earth data and AI to support sustainable farming and crop rotation decisions. I’m looking for teammates skilled in Python, AI/ML, web development, data science, GIS, agriculture, or UI/UX. Most importantly, I value creativity, teamwork, curiosity, and a willingness to learn!
summary: Earth Intelligence AI (Earth System Trend Detective) turns NASA Earth observation data into plain-English environmental answers. Many people can see satellite data but cannot tell whether a change is real or just noise. Our Streamlit app takes monthly NASA time series for heat, rain and soil moisture for a 25 km box around Chennai (2002–2025). It removes the seasonal cycle and tests each trend with Sen’s slope, the Hamed-Rao modified Mann-Kendall test and a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. It then compares the three signals with Pearson correlations. Results are explained in plain English with a clear “significant or not” verdict, using “may indicate” and never “caused by”. For Chennai, none of the three trends is statistically significant, and heat and soil moisture are negatively correlated (r = −0.57), which does not prove cause. Finding no significant trend is a valid result, and a longer record may help. The app is open source and live.
details:
What it does. Earth Intelligence AI is a Streamlit app that detects the direction and size of change in heat, rain and soil moisture, shows how the signals move together, and explains the result in plain English. Pages: Start here, Detective (a guided 3-step question picker), Result (verdict banner, trend line, anomaly chart, slope per decade, p-value and 95% interval), Connect the signals, Demo examples, and Method and limits.

How it works. We collect monthly series from NASA Giovanni, clean them and convert units (K to °C, precipitation to mm per month), and remove fill values. We remove the seasonal cycle to get monthly anomalies. We test the trend with Sen’s slope and the Hamed-Rao modified Mann-Kendall test, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval, and compare the signals with Pearson correlations.

Findings (Chennai, 2002–2025). Heat: −0.035 °C per decade (p = 0.80). Rain: +5.4 mm per decade (p = 0.21). Soil moisture: −3.1 kg m⁻² per decade (p = 0.49). None is statistically significant. Heat and soil moisture are negatively correlated (r = −0.57), which does not prove cause.

Benefits and impact. It makes trend statistics easier for researchers, communities and decision-makers who lack remote-sensing expertise to understand. It reports honestly when a trend is not significant.

Tools. Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, Plotly, GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud.

Limits and future scope. GLDAS is a model, skin temperature is not air temperature, and the box is about 25 km. Future work: more regions with a region picker, MODIS NDVI via AppEEARS, Landsat land-cover checks, longer records, and AI-written reports grounded in the computed numbers.
